nameStory: The six-spotted fishing spider gets its name from the distinctive light spots on its abdomen and its remarkable ability to fish for aquatic prey. Like an eight-legged angler, this spider can actually walk on water and dive beneath the surface to catch small fish, tadpoles, and aquatic insects. Its scientific name 'triton' honors the Greek sea god Triton, messenger of the ocean and son of Poseidon.
description: The six-spotted fishing spider is a large, impressive arachnid that looks like it belongs on the water rather than on land. These robust spiders have dark brown to grayish bodies with six prominent light spots arranged in two rows along their abdomen. They're among New England's largest spiders, with females reaching leg spans that can cover the palm of your hand. Their long, powerful legs are perfectly adapted for skimming across pond surfaces like natural water-skippers.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Six distinct light-colored spots arranged in two neat rows along the dark abdomen, like decorative buttons on a vest

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits at water's edge with front legs touching the surface, feeling for vibrations; can run across water without sinking

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Robust, sturdy build with a velvety-textured abdomen and thick, muscular legs that feel substantial if handled

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large spider with females having leg spans reaching 3+ inches; body feels surprisingly heavy and solid compared to house spiders

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found near water - perched on logs, rocks, or vegetation at pond edges, boat docks, or stream margins

habitat: Six-spotted fishing spiders inhabit the edges of ponds, lakes, slow streams, and marshes throughout New England's wetlands. Look for them on wooden boat docks, fallen logs, emergent cattails, and rocky shorelines where they can easily access both land and water. They prefer areas with calm water and plenty of vegetation that provides both hunting grounds and quick escape routes.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots under logs and bark near water. Mating season begins, with males cautiously approaching females on lily pads and dock edges.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting at water's edge. Females carry large, round egg sacs that look like gray pearls attached to their spinnerets.
seasonality.fall: Spiderlings disperse from their mothers and can be seen as miniature versions near water. Adults seek overwintering sites under loose bark and in rock crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected spots near their aquatic habitats, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns them to active hunting.

funFact: These spiders can actually dive underwater and stay submerged for up to 30 minutes, breathing air trapped in the fine hairs covering their bodies - essentially wearing their own diving suit made of tiny air bubbles!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the larger Dark Fishing Spider, but the six white spots are the dead giveaway - count the spots and you'll know for sure. Remember: 'Six spots, six-spotted' - the Dark Fishing Spider has white stripes along its sides instead of the neat row of spots.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their intimidating size and the word 'fishing' in their name, these spiders are completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial, controlling mosquito populations around water bodies. The 'dock spider' nickname comes from their habit of disappearing into the cracks between dock boards when startled.
compareHints: The six-spotted fishing spider is distinguished from its close relative the Dark Fishing Spider by its characteristic six light spots versus the Dark Fishing Spider's white side stripes. The Striped Fishing Spider has more extensive light markings covering much of its body, while the six-spotted keeps its light markings confined to those telltale six abdominal spots.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the striped fishing spider and six-spotted fishing spider which are typically found near water and have more contrasting markings, the dark fishing spider has subtler coloration and lives almost exclusively on trees.

Among New England's fishing spiders, the Striped Fishing Spider is distinguished by its pale brown coloration with prominent light stripes, while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker and larger, and the Six-spotted Fishing Spider has distinctive white spots instead of stripes.
Among New England's fishing spiders, the Banded Fishing Spider is distinguished by its bold, regular light bands across a dark body.
Among New England's fishing spiders, striatus has the most clearly defined striped patterns - other species like the dark fishing spider have more mottled or spotted appearances.

The white-banded fishing spider stands out from its fishing spider relatives by having the most clearly defined white bands - the dark fishing spider has more subdued, mottled markings, while the striped fishing spider shows yellowish stripes rather than bright white bands.
